# Fire, Garbage, and Recycling

The oldest name we know may belong to an accountant.

There is a clay tablet from Uruk, in what is now southern Iraq, roughly five thousand years old. It is about the size of a bar of soap. Pressed into it are wedge-shaped marks recording a quantity of barley — something like twenty-nine thousand measures over thirty-seven months — and then a sign that scholars read as *Kushim*. Not a king. Not a god. Possibly not even a person; it might be a title, or an office, or the name of an institution. But if it is a person, then the first human being whose name survives anywhere in the world spent his life counting grain, and the second thing he ever wrote down was his own signature.

People find this disappointing. Writing ought to have begun with a hymn, or a love letter, or a king boasting about a battle. Instead it began with inventory. For centuries before anyone thought to write down a story, scribes in Mesopotamia were recording sheep, beer, sesame oil, rations for workers, the delivery of reeds. One influential theory holds that the whole technology grew out of small clay tokens sealed inside hollow clay balls — a shipping manifest you had to break open to read — until someone realized you could just impress the shapes on the outside and skip the ball entirely. Writing, on this account, is a compression artifact of packaging.

I find this consoling rather than deflating, and the reason is the tablet itself. It survived. It survived because it was made of mud, and mud is nearly worthless, and nobody bothered to destroy it, and the sun baked it, and the sand covered it. It survived because it was garbage that happened to be made of stone.

Almost everything we know about the deep past arrived by that route. Not because someone treasured it. Because it was durable, or discarded, or recycled — and because, quite often, a building burned down.

---

Consider the two great writing materials of the ancient world. Papyrus is beautiful, light, portable, and doomed. It rots in damp air. It is eaten by insects. Outside of exceptional conditions — the Egyptian desert, a sealed cave, a volcanic accident — a papyrus roll has a life expectancy measured in centuries at best, and usually much less. Clay is heavy, clumsy, limited to short texts, and effectively immortal. Fire does not destroy it. Fire *improves* it.

This produces one of the great ironies of archaeology. When an enemy army sacked a Bronze Age or Iron Age palace, killed everyone in it, and torched the buildings, the flames baked the unbaked administrative tablets in the records office and turned them into ceramics. The destruction of the civilization is the reason we can read its paperwork.

Nineveh fell in 612 BCE. Ashurbanipal's library — the great deliberate collection, the one with the flood story and the epic of Gilgamesh in it — was buried in the burning ruins and came out harder than it went in. Two and a half millennia later, excavators pulled tens of thousands of fragments out of the mound and started joining them, and we recovered a literature that had been completely forgotten.

The same thing happened across the Aegean around 1200 BCE, when the Mycenaean palaces burned. At Pylos, in the first days of excavation in 1939, diggers hit a room full of clay tablets, sun-dried and thus, in the ordinary course of things, destined to dissolve into the hillside. The fire that ended that world had fired them like pottery.

They were deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an architect who had been obsessed with the script since he was a schoolboy, and who cracked it by treating it as a cryptogram rather than a language problem. It turned out to be Greek — an older Greek than anyone had written down before. And what does the earliest Greek literature say?

It says: *wool*. It says: *sheep, 100*. It says: chariot wheels, missing an axle; a deficit in bronze; quantities of perfumed oil; a list of men assigned to watch the coast. There is not one poem. Not one prayer that we can be sure is a prayer, not one letter home, not one joke. An entire civilization's writing survives, and it is all spreadsheets, because the poems were sung and the spreadsheets were filed in a room that caught fire.

So when we say the Mycenaeans were a bureaucratic palace culture obsessed with the redistribution of commodities, we should hold that thought loosely. We are looking at a burned filing cabinet and calling it a soul.

---

The second great preserver is refuse.

In the 1890s, two young Oxford men, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, went to Egypt and started digging into the rubbish mounds outside a provincial town called Oxyrhynchus. The town had thrown its waste paper into the desert for centuries, and the desert had kept it. They shipped home hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments — tax receipts, contracts, petitions, private letters, invitations to dinner parties, a complaint from a boy named Theon to his father, who had gone off to the city without taking him, informing him that if he wasn't collected soon he would stop eating and stop writing.

Mixed in with the paperwork were pieces of books the town had thrown out when they wore out. Sappho, of whom the Middle Ages retained a handful of quotations, came back in tattered strips. Fragments of a gospel nobody had ever heard of, the Gospel of Thomas, turned up in the first season's boxes. One of the oldest surviving bits of Euclid was in a heap of trash. Menander, a comic playwright so admired in antiquity that he was ranked with Homer, had vanished almost completely — for centuries he existed only as lines quoted by other men — and then papyri began returning him in chunks.

Some of this material survived in an even stranger form. Papyrus was expensive enough that used papyrus had a second life as cardboard. Egyptian undertakers made mummy masks and chest coverings out of layers of glued-together scrap paper, painted over. Which means there are lost books inside funeral equipment, and modern researchers have developed ways to separate the layers or image the ink through the gesso — at the cost, sometimes, of destroying the mask. We are now dismantling one category of artifact to read another. The past is not a warehouse. It is a closed economy in which everything was already reused once.

---

The third preserver is a rule about garbage.

In the synagogue of Ben Ezra in Old Cairo there was a storeroom, a *genizah*. Jewish law forbids destroying a text that contains the name of God, and by long custom the rule was extended generously: worn-out prayer books, defective scrolls, and eventually more or less any writing in Hebrew characters, since Hebrew letters could spell the Name. You did not burn them. You put them in the room. Eventually you buried the room's contents, but the room at Fustat went on accumulating for something like a thousand years.

Nobody was building a library. That is the whole point. A library selects; a genizah accepts. And because the community wrote its secular documents in Judeo-Arabic — Arabic in Hebrew script — the sacred rule accidentally covered the profane. Shopping lists went in. Marriage contracts and divorce proceedings. Bills of lading. Business letters from merchants trading with India, complaining about a shipment, sending regards, asking after someone's health. Children's alphabet practice, the same letter repeated down a page in a wobbling hand. Pages in Maimonides' own handwriting, crossed out and revised, which is to say: the man thinking.

In 1896 two Scottish sisters, Agnes Smith Lewis and Margaret Dunlop Gibson — widows, self-taught in languages, formidable travelers — came back from Egypt with a fragment of a Hebrew text that scholars had believed lost. Solomon Schechter went to Cairo, saw the room, and eventually brought something like a hundred and forty thousand fragments to Cambridge. Across all the collections the total is usually estimated around three hundred thousand pieces.

The result is the most complete record of ordinary daily life anywhere in the medieval world. Not because anyone valued ordinary daily life. Because a rule about the disposal of sacred objects created, as a side effect, an archive that could not filter.

---

Then there is recycling in its purest form: parchment scraped clean and written on again.

A sheepskin is expensive. A monastery with a shortage of skins and a surplus of old books had an obvious solution: wash and scrape the ink off a volume nobody read anymore, and use it for something useful. The result is a palimpsest, from the Greek for *scraped again*. Usually the newer text won completely. But iron-gall ink bites into the skin, and traces stay in the follicles, and if you light the page correctly — ultraviolet, multispectral imaging, X-ray fluorescence — the older writing rises up underneath like a watermark.

The most spectacular example is a thirteenth-century prayer book in Jerusalem that turned out to be built on top of tenth-century copies of Archimedes. Under the prayers is the *Method of Mechanical Theorems*, in which Archimedes explains how he actually discovered things, as opposed to how he proved them — a text nobody had seen for a thousand years, and the only surviving copy. Under the prayers is also the *Stomachion*, a combinatorial puzzle, and the only Greek text of *On Floating Bodies*, and speeches by the Athenian orator Hyperides that had been entirely lost. A prayer book had been made out of the wreckage of mathematics and pagan rhetoric, and the monks who made it had, without intending to, kept both alive.

The reverse also happens. In 1819 the Vatican librarian Angelo Mai found substantial parts of Cicero's *De re publica* under a commentary Augustine had written on the Psalms — a genuine recovery of a major lost work. Mai was celebrated. He was also prolific, and impatient, and he treated his manuscripts with chemical reagents to bring up the faded ink. The reagents worked, briefly, and then darkened. Later scholars found pages that had been legible before he saved them and were now black. The instinct to recover and the impulse to destroy are not opposites; they run on the same fuel.

---

Set against all of this is the other channel: deliberate copying.

Some texts survived not by accident but because generations of people chose to recopy them, hand to hand, century to century, in an unbroken relay. This is how we have Homer and Virgil and most of the Bible. It is a far more faithful channel than a rubbish heap. It is also brutally narrow, because copying is expensive, and what gets copied is what somebody has a reason to copy: what schools teach, what lawyers cite, what a religious community needs, what a rich patron likes.

Aeschylus wrote perhaps eighty plays. We have seven. Sophocles wrote around a hundred and twenty; seven survive. Euripides wrote about ninety; we have eighteen or nineteen. And there is a strange pattern in which nineteen: ten of them fall in alphabetical order, from *Helen* through *Ion* to *Iphigeneia*. Scholars suspect this is not chance — that what came down to us was one volume of a collected edition, the E-to-K volume, the part of the shelf that happened to make it into a schoolroom in late antiquity while the other volumes quietly rotted. Not the best plays. The middle of the alphabet.

So we have two channels, biased in opposite directions. Deliberate transmission preserves what an elite thought worth teaching. Accident preserves whatever was cheap, unwanted, and thrown into a dry place. Between them lies almost everything: the songs people actually sang, the arguments in the street, what a woman thought about her marriage, the joke that made a whole tavern laugh in 400 BCE. We are not reading the past. We are reading its tax office and its syllabus, and inferring a world.

---

Which brings me to the part that ought to worry us.

We are producing more text than any civilization in history, and we are putting essentially all of it on the most fragile medium ever devised. Not fragile in the way papyrus is fragile — papyrus at least sits still and waits. A hard drive fails. A tape demagnetizes. A file format loses its last reader. And a digital document is not an object you can look at; it is a set of instructions that requires a functioning machine, an operating system, an application, and a codec, all of which are moving targets. Clay needs eyes and a trained mind. A 1995 word-processing file needs an entire industrial civilization to still be running.

The standard cautionary tale is almost too neat. In 1986, for the nine-hundredth anniversary of the Domesday Book, the BBC made its own Domesday: a survey of Britain contributed to by around a million people, with photographs and text and maps, stored on interactive laserdiscs and playable on a specific microcomputer. It was a marvel. Within about fifteen years it was essentially unreadable — the discs were fine, the machines and software were gone. A rescue effort had to be mounted, involving emulation and reverse engineering, to get the data back out.

The original Domesday Book, made of ink on animal skin in 1086, remains readable by anyone who can read Latin. No machine required. No institution required. Just a person and a page.

---

The most hopeful thing I know about all this is happening in a carbonized lump from Herculaneum.

When Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, a pyroclastic surge hit a villa with a library in it and cooked roughly eighteen hundred papyrus scrolls into black cylinders that look like burnt sausages. They were found in the 1750s. For two and a half centuries people tried to read them, mostly by unrolling them, which mostly destroyed them. Early attempts split scrolls into strips, sliced them, treated them with mercury; a great deal of what was left of that library was consumed by the effort to read it.

Then came the obvious-in-hindsight idea: don't open it. Scan it. The trouble is that the ink is carbon and the papyrus is carbon, so a CT scan sees no contrast at all — the writing is invisible in the data. But the ink sits on the surface with a subtly different texture, a faint crackle, and that texture can be learned. In 2023, using synchrotron scans and machine learning, a student found a word in an unopened scroll: *porphyras*. Purple. Months later a team recovered continuous passages — a discussion of pleasure, of food and music and the things we pursue, from a library of Epicurean philosophy that has been shut since the reign of Titus.

A book was read without being opened, by people who will never touch the page.

I keep turning that over, because it points at what actually matters here. We obsess over durable objects — archival paper, etched nickel discs, vaults in Arctic mountains. But durability was never the binding constraint. Clay is durable and Linear A is still unread: we can pronounce the signs, more or less, and have no idea what the words mean. The Indus script sits mute, four thousand short inscriptions with no bilingual and no known language family behind it. The Rosetta Stone worked for one reason, and it wasn't the granite. It was that Greek never stopped being taught.

What carries the past across time is not a tough material. It is an unbroken chain of people who know how to read, and who bother to teach the next ones. The bequest that matters isn't the artifact; it's the reader. Which means the real act of preservation, right now, is not carving something into a mountain. It's making sure somebody, in a hundred years, still knows what to do with what we left — and still wants to.

Kushim got lucky. Mud, fire, sand, and then four thousand years of people learning to read wedges. Only one of those was his doing.
